title: SOLID Principles
description: SOLID is an acronym for five fundamental principles of object-oriented design, introduced by Robert C. Martin. Applied together they make software more maintainable, flexible and understandable, and reduce code smells and technical debt.

principles.name: Single Responsibility Principle
principles.definition: A class should have only one reason to change.
key_concepts: Each class should have a single responsibility or purpose
"Reason to change" refers to a specific stakeholder or functionality requirement
Promotes high cohesion and easier maintenance
Makes code more testable and less prone to bugs

bad_practice.title: Violation of SRP

good_practice.title: Following SRP

benefits: Improved maintenance: changes to one responsibility don't affect others
Better testability: smaller, focused classes are easier to test
Reduced coupling: fewer dependencies between components
Enhanced readability: a clear purpose for each class
Easier to modify without affecting other parts of the system
indicators_of_violation: Class has multiple unrelated methods
Methods operate on different data within the class
The class changes for multiple reasons
Describing the class's purpose requires the word "and" or "or"
Changes to one feature require modifying multiple classes
principles.spring_usage: Spring leverages stereotypes (@Service, @Repository, @Controller) to encourage responsibility segregation. Services hold business logic, repositories manage data access, controllers handle HTTP concerns.

interview_question.question: How do you implement the Single Responsibility Principle in your projects?
interview_question.answer:
I implement SRP by:
- Creating smaller, focused classes with clear purposes
- Separating concerns into their respective layers (repository for data access, service for business logic)
- Using composition to combine functionality without bloating classes
- Refactoring when I notice a class has multiple responsibilities or reasons to change

For example, in a Spring application, instead of one large service class handling user management, email notifications and report generation, I'd create separate UserService, NotificationService and ReportService classes.

principles.name: Open-Closed Principle
principles.definition: Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.
key_concepts: Design classes so that you can add new functionality without changing existing code
Use abstractions (interfaces and abstract classes) to enable extension
Implement polymorphism to allow varying behavior
Focus on creating stable interfaces

bad_practice.title: Violation of OCP

good_practice.title: Following OCP

benefits: Reduced risk: changes to existing, working functionality are minimized
Easier maintenance: new features arrive as extensions, not modifications
Better testability: core functionality remains stable
Cleaner architecture: clear separation between stable abstractions and changing implementations
indicators_of_violation: Large conditional statements (if/else chains, switch on a type code)
Frequent modifications to existing classes to add new features
Difficulty extending functionality without editing existing code
Tightly coupled classes with high dependencies
principles.spring_usage: Spring's BeanFactoryPostProcessor and BeanPostProcessor let you extend container behavior without modifying core code, and Aspect-Oriented Programming adds cross-cutting behavior without changing existing classes.

interview_question.question: How does the Open-Closed Principle relate to interfaces and abstract classes?
interview_question.answer:
OCP guides us to design software so new functionality can be added without modifying existing code. Interfaces and abstract classes make that possible by:
- Providing stable contracts that clients can depend on
- Allowing new implementations to be added without changing existing code
- Enabling polymorphic behavior where new classes can be used in place of existing ones
- Creating explicit extension points for plugins or modules

For instance, by defining a PaymentProcessor interface we can add new payment methods (Bitcoin, Apple Pay) without touching the existing payment flow.

principles.name: Liskov Substitution Principle
principles.definition: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program.
key_concepts: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without breaking functionality
Subclasses should extend the capabilities of the parent class without reducing them
Subclasses should not change the behavior expected of the superclass
Preserve the invariants of the superclass

bad_practice.title: Violation of LSP

good_practice.title: Following LSP

benefits: Predictable behavior: code written against the base class works with any subclass
Logical hierarchy: class relationships reflect real substitutability
Reduced bugs: fewer surprises when using polymorphism
Better abstraction: clear separation of common and specific behavior
indicators_of_violation: Throwing exceptions in subclass methods that the superclass contract doesn't allow
Overriding a method to do nothing, or with unrelated behavior
Type checking before method calls (instanceof checks)
Subclasses that weaken preconditions or strengthen postconditions
principles.spring_usage: Spring's ApplicationContext implementations are freely substitutable, and Spring Data repository interfaces preserve substitutability across the generated implementations.

interview_question.question: What's a real example of the Liskov Substitution Principle being violated?
interview_question.answer:
The classic example is the Rectangle-Square problem:
- A Rectangle has width and height that can be set independently
- A Square is a special Rectangle where width equals height
- If Square extends Rectangle but overrides setWidth() to set both dimensions, it violates client expectations
- Code that works with Rectangle can break with Square, even though mathematically a square is a rectangle

This violates LSP because Square doesn't honour Rectangle's behavioral contract. A better design separates the hierarchy or uses composition instead of inheritance.

principles.name: Interface Segregation Principle
principles.definition: Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use.
key_concepts: Create smaller, more specific interfaces rather than large general-purpose ones
Classes should only implement the methods they actually need
Favor role interfaces over header interfaces
Prevent "interface pollution", where implementations are forced to provide irrelevant methods

bad_practice.title: Violation of ISP

good_practice.title: Following ISP

benefits: Improved clarity: interfaces define clear roles and expectations
Better client focus: clients depend only on what they need
Reduced coupling: changes to unused methods don't affect clients
Higher cohesion: interfaces represent meaningful clusters of related functionality
indicators_of_violation: Interfaces with many unrelated methods
Methods throwing UnsupportedOperationException
Classes implementing methods they don't need or use
Clients using only a small subset of a large interface
principles.spring_usage: Spring defines many focused interfaces rather than one large one: JpaRepository and CrudRepository in Spring Data, and UserDetailsService, AuthenticationProvider and friends in Spring Security.

interview_question.question: How do you identify violations of the Interface Segregation Principle?
interview_question.answer:
I look for:
- Large interfaces with methods that aren't implemented by all classes
- Implementations throwing UnsupportedOperationException
- Classes implementing an interface but using only a small subset of its methods
- Clients that call only a few methods of a large interface

When I find these, I refactor by splitting the interface into smaller, cohesive interfaces that each represent a specific capability or role.

principles.name: Dependency Inversion Principle
principles.definition: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. Abstractions should not depend on details — details should depend on abstractions.
key_concepts: Create stable interfaces between the layers of your application
High-level policy should not depend on low-level implementation details
Use dependency injection to supply implementations to higher-level components
Define abstractions that capture essential behavior without committing to a specific implementation

bad_practice.title: Violation of DIP

good_practice.title: Following DIP

benefits: Flexibility: change implementations without affecting clients
Testability: easy to supply mock implementations in tests
Maintainability: fewer cascading changes when an implementation changes
Modularity: clearly defined boundaries between components
indicators_of_violation: Direct instantiation of implementation classes with new
Concrete class references where an interface would do
High-level modules affected by changes in low-level modules
Difficulty unit-testing because dependencies are concrete
principles.spring_usage: Dependency injection is the core Spring feature. Beans are wired through abstractions rather than concrete implementations; constructor injection is the idiomatic way to follow DIP.

interview_question.question: What's the difference between Dependency Inversion and Dependency Injection?
interview_question.answer:
Dependency Inversion is a principle (the "D" in SOLID): high-level modules should depend on abstractions, not on details.

Dependency Injection is a pattern for implementing DIP. It works by:
- Providing dependencies to a class rather than letting the class create them
- Moving responsibility for constructing dependencies outside the class
- Making testing easier, since mock dependencies can be injected

In short, DIP tells you what to do (depend on abstractions) and DI is one way to do it (inject those abstractions).

spring_framework.example: Using @Service, @Repository and @Controller annotations to separate concerns
Using interfaces plus dependency injection, and AOP/BeanPostProcessor extension points
Swapping Spring Data repository implementations behind the same interface
Narrow, role-based interfaces such as CrudRepository, UserDetailsService and AuthenticationProvider
The Spring IoC container and constructor-based dependency injection

microservices.question: How do SOLID principles apply to microservices architecture?
microservices.answer:
SOLID scales up from classes to services:
- SRP: each microservice owns a single responsibility or domain
- OCP: new functionality arrives as new services rather than edits to existing ones
- LSP: service interfaces stay consistent, so one implementation can replace another
- ISP: service APIs are focused on specific client needs rather than being overly general
- DIP: services communicate through abstractions (contracts, APIs) rather than concrete implementations

Together these produce loosely coupled, highly cohesive services that can evolve independently.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A class should only have one method
common_misconceptions.clarification: The principle is about having one responsibility or reason to change, not about the number of methods
You can modify code to fix bugs or improve an implementation, but new features should be added through extension

common_misconceptions.misconception: If the compiler accepts the subclass, LSP is satisfied
common_misconceptions.clarification: LSP is about behavior, not types. A subclass can compile perfectly and still break callers by throwing where the base class never throws, or by changing the meaning of a method

common_misconceptions.misconception: Dependency Inversion and Dependency Injection are the same thing
common_misconceptions.clarification: DIP is the principle (depend on abstractions); DI is one technique for achieving it. You can use a DI framework and still violate DIP by injecting concrete classes

considerations: Consider team experience and project constraints
Start with the most relevant principle for your problem
best_practices: Start with simpler principles like SRP before tackling more complex ones like DIP
Refactor toward SOLID gradually rather than attempting a complete overhaul
Use SOLID as a design guide, not just as a way to fix problems after the fact
Consider trade-offs with other qualities such as performance and simplicity
Combine SOLID with design patterns for more effective solutions
Use automated tools (linters, static analyzers) to detect potential violations
Review code regularly to identify opportunities for SOLID improvements

interview_questions.question: What are the SOLID principles and why are they important?
interview_questions.answer:
SOLID is five design principles that guide object-oriented programming toward more maintainable, flexible and understandable software. They matter because they:
- Make code easier to maintain and extend
- Reduce technical debt and code smells
- Improve testability and reusability
- Provide a common vocabulary for discussing software design

interview_questions.question: Are there cases where it's acceptable to violate SOLID principles?
interview_questions.answer:
Yes — SOLID principles are guidelines, not absolute rules. Acceptable trade-offs include:
- Simplicity: following SOLID strictly can add unnecessary complexity to a simple application
- Performance: abstractions add indirection that may be unacceptable in performance-critical code
- Small scope: for small, non-critical utilities or scripts, full SOLID compliance may not be worth the overhead
- Legacy integration: when working with legacy code, perfect adherence is often impractical

The key is making a conscious, informed decision about when to trade SOLID compliance for other values — not violating them by accident.
